text: Clap your hands once...
in a vast cathedral.
That single sharp clap comes back as a fading
trail of echoes:
one... point six...
point three... point one.
Now, play two notes in a row:
a quiet two, then a louder three.
Each note launches its own echo trail.
At step one, what you actually hear is the
vertical sum: yesterday's fading echo,
one point two...
plus today's fresh note,
three... giving four point two.
Blending an input with an echo is called convolution.
But look at the textbook formula:
why is the echo written backwards,
as n minus k?
Nature never flips the echo in time.
It happens because newest inputs hit the fresh head
of the echo, h zero...
while older inputs hit the older tail,
h one and h two.
So, if we take our echo strip and flip
it end for end...
every matching pair lines up in the same vertical column.
Let's try it with real numbers:
one, two, three, convolved with four,
five, six. First...
flip four, five, six into six, five, four.
Now slide it across.
First touch: one times four is four.
Next step: five plus eight gives thirteen.
Full overlap in the center:
six plus ten plus twelve peaks at twenty-eight! Then
twenty-seven... and finally, eighteen.
What if our strip holds weights that add up
to one— like a quarter,
a half, and a quarter?
Sliding it across a noisy signal averages neighboring points
into a smooth curve.
Shrink those steps until they become infinitely thin...
and the sum melts into a smooth shaded area:
the continuous convolution integral.
In two dimensions, our sliding strip becomes a three-by-three
window scanning across an image.
When all nine weights are one-ninth,
sharp jumps blend into a soft blur.
Now put negative weights on the left,
and positive on the right.
Flat patches cancel to zero...
while the vertical boundary lights up bright.
Here is the twist in modern AI.
Deep learning libraries actually skip the one-hundred-eighty-degree
flip, and compute cross-correlation instead.
Because a neural network learns its filter weights from
data, it simply learns them already flipped.
One big idea connects them all:
flip... slide... multiply... and sum.
